The Hebrew range (hebrew.py root אמן: he'emin 'believe', niphal 'be firm', emunah 'steadiness/fidelity', emet 'firmness, truth', amen; Aramaic mehēman 'trustworthy') shares both faces the page develops: entering security and being reliable. Isa 7:9 puns believe/be established (¶4); Gen 15:1,6 joins removal of fear and belief (¶6); Exod 17:12 emunah = steady hands, Dan 6:5 Aramaic 'trustworthy' (¶7); Gen 45:26 he'emin in the brothers' report scene (¶9, counter-narrative); amen as answer formula, Deut 27:15, Jer 28:6 (¶9); emet in Zech 8:16 shows the Hebrew word for truth in the same root (¶22); Hab 2:4 emunah (¶36). Isa 26:3, Jer 17:7, Ps 37:3 use bṭḥ, not this root.

Sound correspondence only. BDB gives ḥāqaq 'cut in, inscribe, decree' and ḥōq 'something prescribed, a statute or due'. Only the 'due/allotted share' sense meets the Arabic haqq of ¶23 (Lev 10:13 'your due and your sons' due', Prov 30:8 'my allotted bread'); the statute (Deut 4:8, Exod 18:20, Ps 119:5), engraving (Job 19:23) and boundary (Prov 8:29) senses do not carry the page's 'truth/fit' sense, and Hebrew expresses truth with emet (אמן) instead.

חסר (sound correspondence only): 'lack, be lacking, decrease'; Aramaic ḥassîr 'found wanting' on the scales (Dan 5:27) is a real and apt use, and Ps 23:1, Deut 2:7, Prov 11:24, 28:27 use the root for want. But khusr is the word of 103:2; on this page it appears only as a cross-reference (¶12, ¶23), so no block was placed here. חשר: BDB's Arabic note concerns a different Arabic root (collect), not خسر; false friend in form only.

Sound correspondence only. Hebrew ṣābar means only 'heap up' (8 occurrences: Gen 41:35,49; Exod 8:10; 2 Kgs 10:8; Job 27:16; Ps 39:7; Hab 1:10; Zech 9:3); the patience sense is absent, so for the ayah's sabr it is a false friend, but it meets the 'unweighed heap' sense of ¶35. Gen 41:49 (grain heaped beyond counting) is used there; Job 27:16 and Ps 39:7 duplicate it.

Sound correspondence only. Hebrew ṣālēaḥ mostly 'advance, prosper' (Gen 39, Josh 1:8, Ps 1:3, 2 Chr 20:20; Aramaic Ezra 6:14 'prosper') and ṣālaḥ 'rush (of the spirit)'; these success senses differ from Arabic ṣalāḥ. In Jer 13:7,10 and Ezek 15:4 the verb means 'be fit/useful' and stands beside נִשְׁחַת 'ruined', matching ¶13's salah as the opposite of corruption; used there.

Sound correspondence only (BDB: ʿāṣar 'restrain, retain'; maʿṣār 'restraint, control', Pr 25:28; ʿăṣārâ 'assembly'). The Hebrew root lacks the Arabic time/afternoon and pressing senses but shares 'holding back', which ¶29 cites for al-ʿaṣr. Gen 16:2 (restrained by another) and Prov 25:28 (no restraint over one's spirit) show both directions named in ¶29. 1 Kgs 8:35 (heavens shut) and Ps 106:30 (plague stayed) are other senses, not used.

Sound correspondence only. Hebrew ʿāmal/ʿāmāl = toil, trouble, wearisome labour (55 of 76 occurrences the noun; concentrated in Qohelet, Job, Psalms), not the intentional 'act' of Arabic ʿamal. The difference is the point of the ¶10 block: Qohelet asks what gain (yitron) toil brings (1:3) and finds none (2:11), except where two labour together (4:9-10).

The table lists no correspondence and this lexicon edition gives no cognate note; צוה (ṣiwwâ 'charge, command', miṣwâ) is proposed from knowledge as a possible counterpart with weak radicals in another order, unverified. The block says so and rests only on semantic range: like waṣṣā/waṣiyya, ṣiwwâ covers both binding command and the dying man's charge (Isa 38:1 'charge your house, for you will die'; Gen 49:33; also Gen 18:19 yeṣawweh, used at ¶20).
